presentingComplaint: Progressive jaundice, dark urine and right-upper-quadrant discomfort for 5 days, preceded by a week of fever, nausea and body-aches.
history: Previously healthy construction worker in peri-urban Delhi, living in a colony with an intermittent piped-water supply and recent monsoon flooding of the local supply line; several co-workers had a similar illness. He describes a 7-day prodrome of low-grade fever, marked anorexia, nausea with a few episodes of vomiting, distaste for cigarettes and generalized myalgia, followed by darkening of the urine, pale stools and yellowing of the eyes over the last 5 days as the fever settled. No abdominal distension, confusion, sleep-reversal or bleeding. No blood transfusion, tattoos, injection drug use, high-risk sexual exposure or prior liver disease. Takes no regular medication and specifically denies paracetamol overdose, herbal/ayurvedic hepatotoxins or significant alcohol. He first attended a peripheral clinic where 'fever with jaundice' was labelled possible enteric fever/leptospirosis and empirical IV ceftriaxone was started 3 days ago with no improvement, prompting referral.
examination: Alert, oriented, deeply icteric with icteric sclerae; no asterixis, no fetor hepaticus, no spider naevi, palmar erythema or gynaecomastia to suggest chronic liver disease. Mild tender smooth hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin with a soft palpable spleen tip; no ascites, no shifting dullness, no flank/calf tenderness, no eschar, no conjunctival suffusion, no petechiae. Chest and cardiovascular examination normal.
imaging: USG abdomen: mild smooth hepatomegaly with normal echotexture, oedematous/thick-walled but non-calculous gallbladder (consistent with acute hepatitis), no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary dilatation, patent portal vein, mild splenomegaly, no ascites or focal hepatic lesion — excluding biliary obstruction and liver abscess.
microbiology: Anti-HEV IgM POSITIVE. Anti-HAV IgM negative, HBsAg negative, anti-HBc IgM negative, anti-HCV negative. Peripheral smear for malaria parasite negative x2; dengue NS1/IgM negative; leptospira IgM negative; blood cultures sterile at 48h; urine culture no growth. HEV RNA (confirmatory) pending.
differentialDiagnoses: Leptospirosis (waterborne, myalgia, jaundice — but no conjunctival suffusion/AKI and leptospira IgM negative)
Malaria (tropical fever with jaundice — excluded by two negative smears)
Drug/toxin-induced (toxic) hepatitis — no hepatotoxin, paracetamol or herbal exposure
Acute cholangitis (fever + jaundice + RUQ — excluded by absent biliary dilatation and sterile blood cultures)
finalDiagnosis: Acute viral hepatitis, hepatitis E (icteric phase), self-limiting, without acute liver failure.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Acute Viral Hepatitis
ICMR — Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use in Common Syndromes, 2019
stewardship: This is a viral illness: antibacterials have NO role in uncomplicated acute viral hepatitis. The key stewardship action is to STOP the empirical ceftriaxone started for 'fever with jaundice' once a viral aetiology is confirmed (anti-HEV IgM positive, sterile cultures, no biliary source) — a de-escalation/discontinuation decision, not escalation. Management is supportive: hydration, antiemetics, rest, avoidance of hepatotoxins (paracetamol >2 g/day, alcohol, herbal remedies) and sedatives, with serial monitoring of INR and sensorium to detect evolving acute liver failure. Antibiotics are reserved only for a subsequently documented bacterial complication (e.g., SBP if ascites develops). Counsel on faeco-oral transmission, safe water and hand hygiene.
contraindications: Avoid unnecessary antibacterials — no bacterial source identified
Avoid hepatotoxic drugs (high-dose paracetamol, alcohol, herbal/ayurvedic hepatotonics)
Avoid sedatives/opioids that can precipitate or mask encephalopathy
Avoid nephrotoxic NSAIDs given risk of hepatorenal compromise
edgeCases: Hepatitis E in pregnancy carries a high risk of fulminant hepatic failure and mortality — pregnancy status must be established
Acute HEV superimposed on unrecognised chronic liver disease (acute-on-chronic liver failure)
Chronic hepatitis E in solid-organ transplant/immunocompromised hosts
Rising INR, falling sensorium or shrinking liver span signal progression to acute liver failure requiring transplant-centre referral
expectedMaiK: Recognise self-limiting acute viral hepatitis E, discontinue the inappropriate empirical antibiotics, give supportive care, and monitor INR/sensorium for acute liver failure.
expectedNextQuestions: Source of drinking water and any recent flooding or similar illness in contacts?
Any paracetamol, herbal/ayurvedic remedies, other drugs or alcohol exposure?
Any confusion, altered sleep pattern, or abnormal bleeding?
Risk factors for parenteral/sexual hepatitis B/C exposure and vaccination history?
In a female patient — pregnancy status (HEV in pregnancy is high-risk)?
expectedInvestigations: Acute viral hepatitis serology panel (anti-HEV IgM, anti-HAV IgM, HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV)
LFTs with fractionated bilirubin and transaminases
Prothrombin time / INR (marker of synthetic failure)
USG abdomen to exclude biliary obstruction and focal lesions
Malaria smear, dengue and leptospira serology to exclude mimics
Blood and urine cultures to confirm absence of a bacterial source

investigations: Anti-HEV IgM and full acute hepatitis serology panel

regressionAssertions: Engine returns VIRAL_HEPATITIS as the top diagnosis.
Positive anti-HEV IgM with sterile cultures and no biliary dilatation drives the diagnosis over bacterial/parasitic mimics.
No antibacterial therapy is recommended; empirical ceftriaxone should be stopped.
Markedly elevated transaminases (>1000 U/L) with hepatocellular pattern are recognised as acute viral hepatitis rather than biliary obstruction.
INR and sensorium are flagged for monitoring to detect acute liver failure.
